body: For bitcoin, the June closing low near $58,500 is now the key level. A clean break would put the next on-chain support clusters, around $57,000 and then $47,000, in play, and would probably trigger more selling from miners whose costs sit well above the price. For Strategy shareholders, forced selling by index funds around the November 30 MSCI removal could widen the discount further before any rebound. Heavy options positioning could make moves in either direction more violent. A recovery in the ratio back above 1, as happened in July, would be the clearest sign that sellers are finished. JPMorgan reads Strategy's record discount to its bitcoin holdings as a sign that selling may be nearly exhausted, but ETF outflows, struggling miners and a looming index removal mean the market has yet to confirm a bottom. Strategy, the world's largest corporate holder of bitcoin, has fallen to a record discount to the value of its bitcoin holdings on JPMorgan's preferred measure. The bank's analysts see this as a possible sign that selling in the cryptocurrency is close to capitulation. Several other indicators suggest the bottom may not be in yet. According to BeInCrypto , which reported the findings, the bank's Flows and Liquidity team calculates that the company formerly known as MicroStrategy was valued at 0.88 times its bitcoin holdings on Wednesday. The measure compares the bitcoin holdings with the company's enterprise value, which includes its debt and preferred stock as well as its equity. The previous low of 0.89 came in late June, when bitcoin posted a closing low of around $58,500. The ratio then recovered above 1 by early July. Strategy's own dashboard, which uses a different calculation, shows a reading of around 0.94. Readings this deep tend to reflect extreme pessimism, and similar conditions have often appeared near market lows. There is a complication this time. Strategy is due to be removed from MSCI indexes on November 30, which will force index-tracking funds to sell the shares regardless of value. That could push the discount wider for technical rather than fundamental reasons. Speculative positioning is also unusually heavy. Executive chairman Michael Saylor says outstanding options on the stock equal about 61% of its market value, compared with around 14% for Tesla. The flow picture remains difficult. JPMorgan notes that investors kept pulling money from BlackRock's spot bitcoin ETF even during a brief price rebound, and at a faster pace than in the May to June sell-off. Miners are under strain too. The bank puts the cost of producing one bitcoin at about $86,000, up from $85,000 in September, well above the current price near $60,500. Estimates based on MARA Holdings' filings put costs closer to $63,000, a level the price is now testing. Higher-cost producers may have to sell reserves to stay afloat. Others are more cautious. One crypto research firm says only two of its 13 historical bottom signals had triggered as of November 22, and that after seven similar support breakdowns, the eventual low came at least 17% further down. The head of research at an on-chain analytics firm warned that bottoming and recovery have historically taken months, even with short-term rallies along the way. On-chain cost-basis data points to resistance near $63,000, with around $57,000 seen as the critical threshold below the June low. Deeper support clusters sit near $47,000 and $38,000. For now, the June low near $58,500 is the line to watch. A record discount at Strategy suggests sellers may be close to exhausted, but the market has not yet confirmed a bottom. body: The muted reaction suggests NZD traders are pricing politics as noise unless talks break down. The tail risk is a failed negotiation and a fresh election, which would bring a longer period of uncertainty and could weigh on the currency and New Zealand government bonds. Coalition deals that come with large fiscal commitments are the other thing to watch, especially for bond yields. Outside Wellington, the kiwi remains tied to global risk sentiment and the US dollar. With the Fed widely expected to hike in December and AI-related volatility still unsettling equities, those forces are likely to outweigh the election result. New Zealand's official count has confirmed a hung parliament, but the kiwi's small rise suggests currency traders see coalition talks as a political puzzle rather than an economic threat, at least for now. The New Zealand dollar edged higher on Friday after official election results confirmed a hung parliament. The modest move suggests currency traders see little immediate economic risk in the drawn-out coalition talks that now lie ahead. The final count from the Electoral Commission left the incumbent centre-right coalition short of a majority on its own, so it will need the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to govern. The result removes some of the uncertainty that hung over the preliminary election-night tally, even if it doesn't yet settle who will form the next government. The kiwi's gain of a few points was small by any measure, and the lack of a sharper reaction is telling. Political uncertainty in New Zealand rarely moves the currency for long, and markets appear to be treating the result as a question of coalition arithmetic rather than a shift in economic direction. Having a centrist kingmaker, rather than a party on either ideological flank, may also limit concern about abrupt changes to fiscal policy. The risks haven't disappeared. Negotiations could stretch on for weeks, and if no workable government emerges, New Zealand could face a fresh election. A prolonged stalemate, or a deal that came with significant spending or tax commitments, could test the currency and the local bond market. For now, though, traders seem content to wait. In the meantime, the kiwi's direction is likely to depend on more familiar drivers. Global risk appetite has been fragile amid turmoil in AI-linked stocks, and the New Zealand dollar, like its Australian counterpart, tends to struggle when investors retreat from risk. The US dollar has been supported by expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Moves in those markets, along with the outlook for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, are likely to matter more for the kiwi in the coming days than developments in Wellington. Traders will watch for any signs of progress in coalition talks, but unless the politics turn messy, the election looks set to remain a sideshow for the currency. body: Households' inflation expectations have fallen sharply from their April peak, which eases one worry for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. That leans slightly against any hawkish shift in the policy outlook and is a mild negative for the New Zealand dollar at the margin. The survey's market impact is usually small, though, and moves in global risk appetite and the US dollar are likely to matter more for the currency. The main sensitivity to watch is oil: these readings now follow pump prices closely, so a renewed jump in crude would probably undo much of this month's improvement. Cheaper fuel has pushed Kiwi consumer confidence back above 100 and pulled inflation expectations to a 22-month low, but households still feel better about the future than the present and remain wary of big purchases. New Zealand consumer confidence climbed back above the 100 mark in November. Falling fuel prices pulled households' inflation expectations to their lowest level in nearly two years, and both the current and future measures of sentiment improved. The ANZ-Roy Morgan Consumer Confidence index rose 4 points to 100.2, its strongest reading since January, according to the survey released on Friday. That is still well short of the long-run average of 112, so the recovery from April's low near 80 is not complete. Both components improved. The future conditions index rose to around 111 from 106, while the current conditions index edged up to around 84 from 81. The biggest shift came in inflation expectations. Households now see prices rising 3.9% a year over the next two years, down from 4.2% in October and the lowest since January 2025. That is a steep fall from April's 6.6%, when a spike in pump prices pushed expectations sharply higher. The survey's authors noted that consumers' price expectations fell slightly more than fuel prices over the month, after tracking them almost one-for-one earlier in the year. They also pointed out that inflation expectations and confidence have moved in opposite directions in recent years, which suggests the two are linked. The economic outlook improved but stayed gloomy for the next 12 months. A net 6% of respondents expect bad times for the economy over that period, compared with a net 13% a month earlier. The five-year view rose to a net 16% positive from 8%, close to its long-run average of 19%. Views on household finances were mixed. A net 20% said they were worse off than a year ago, a marginal improvement. A net 22% expect to be better off a year from now, down from 24% but far above April's low of 3%. Appetite for spending remains soft. A net 12% still think it is a bad time to buy a major household item, although that is a 6-point improvement on October. House price expectations rose to 2.3% from 2.0%, still well below the survey's 3.5% average. The survey's authors described the overall mood as below par, citing broader cost-of-living pressures and a soft labour market. They cautioned that consumers' inflation expectations carry less weight for monetary policy than those of businesses, which actually set prices. Households feel better about the future than about the present, which suggests they are not yet ready to spend freely. The next survey is due on December 18. Your market education doesn't end here. The energy needs of planned data centers outstrip planned energy additions in many places where hyperscalers are developing massive campuses. As a result, the private and public sector alike are increasingly and urgently adopting an all-of-the-above approach to energy development, increasing the scale and lifespan of fossil fuels and renewable energies alike, while also pouring funding into the research and development of next-gen energy alternatives. One of those promising energy alternatives is enhanced geothermal. Geothermal energy itself is nothing new – about 85 percent of all houses in Iceland have been heated with geothermal energy for years now. But that kind of geothermal energy is only viable in geologically anomalous places like Iceland, where the heat from the Earth’s core naturally breaks through to the surface in the form of hot springs, geysers, or other forms of heat vents. But the emerging field of enhanced geothermal seeks to make geothermal energy viable anywhere on Earth by digging deep enough to access that heat and pump it to the surface. In order to do that, geothermal startups and research projects are borrowing technology from a sector that knows a whole lot about drilling – Big Oil. That’s right, the next big thing in clean and green energy may come in the form of none other than fracking. Hydraulic fracturing could allow geothermal initiatives to cost-effectively drill to extreme depths where thermal heat is naturally abundant in order to provide a source of zero-emissions energy 24 hours a day, seven days a week. “If you drill down deep enough — three, four, even six kilometers — you reach the point where the crust is uniformly hot,” University of California Irvine engineer Mohammad Javad Abdolhosseini Qomi was quoted in a recent article from the UC Newsroom. “Then you can drill horizontally, create fractures, and pipe in water.” The rock heats the water, turning it to steam that can run turbines that generate electricity. However, we still have a long way to go before that can be achieved at a commercially viable scale. “There is more than enough potential geothermal energy underground to power the entire United States, but unlocking it safely and economically is still a major challenge,” Qomi went on to say. Scientists at the University of California are one of many groups trying to find a pathway toward bringing enhanced geothermal out of lab-based modeling and into the market. Some private companies are likewise working on employing hydraulic fracturing technology to unlock commercial enhanced geothermal. Meanwhile, others are employing techniques from the field of nuclear fusion, using a vacuum-tube gyrotron to vaporize rock molecules with high-frequency electromagnetic waves down a borehole. The round-the-clock energy potential of enhanced geothermal is just one of the sector’s benefits. Another critical advantage of the sector is its broad, bipartisan appeal as one of the vanishingly few forms of clean energy to receive equally enthusiastic policy support under the Biden and Trump administrations. title: BC Securities Commission stays insider trading charges in case linked to former gold junior CFO
summary: Investment fund operator had been charged with two counts of alleged insider trading.
body: Investment fund operator had been charged with two counts of alleged insider trading. The BC Securities Commission said Wednesday that the BC Prosecution Service have stayed charges in an alleged insider trading scheme. Douwe van Hees had been charged in 2025 on two counts of prohibited insider trading under the Criminal Code after an investigation by the BCSC. The investment fund operator had been charged for one count using inside information obtained from Shaun Pollard, who was Chief Financial Officer at Westhaven Gold at the time of the alleged offences and possessed that information by virtue of their employment. Pollard co-founded Westhaven Gold in 2010 and served as its CFO for over 14 years, until February 2025. All charges against Pollard were dropped in October 2025. A second charge was brought against van Hees for using inside information possessed by virtue of van Hees being a shareholder and/or having a business or professional relationship with an issuer. In a May bail hearing in Vancouver Provincial Court, van Hees was granted release on a number of conditions, including that he pay a C$150,000 deposit into court, the BCSC said. Van Hees’ lawyer, Joseph Saulnier of Martland Saulnier, told Business in Vancouver he asked the Commission for a clear statement, but it was not provided. Saulnier also told the newspaper van Hees adamantly maintained his innocence.

title: Brent settles higher as mine strikes, refinery attack stoke Middle East supply concerns - Yahoo Finance
body: CALGARY, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Crude oil prices rose on Thursday after Yemen's Houthis said they hit Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery, and Iran said mines struck ships in the Strait of Hormuz, ‌reviving concerns about supply disruptions. Brent crude futures settled at $96.57 a barrel, up $1.96, or 1.2%. US West Texas ‌Intermediate crude futures, which did not settle on Thursday because of the US Thanksgiving holiday, were up $1.16, or 1.39%, at $84.84 as of 1:21 ​p.m. ET (1821 GMT). A series of events this week increased geopolitical worries and the Middle East risk premium. On Wednesday, the Iran-aligned Houthis said they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, part of a complex that also serves as a major export terminal for Saudi crude. At the same time, shipping has been disrupted through the Strait of Hormuz, where oil ‌supply had been recovering to levels close ⁠to those before the Iran war. On Thursday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two tankers had exploded and caught fire after hitting sea mines north of Oman's Khasab port while attempting ⁠to cross the strait. One of the vessels was a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil, the Guards said. "This is keeping the market on edge into the (Thanksgiving) holiday," said Phil Flynn, senior analyst at Price Futures Group. While data will ​probably ​show a small global supply surplus in October, said Commodity ​Context founder Rory Johnston, the outlook for crude ‌prices is bullish. He cited slowing Hormuz flows, low inventories, and what he called "known, acute risk" to approximately 15% of global supplies. "My view is that we were oversold when (Brent) was dipping below $90," Johnston said. "It was only a matter of time before we tightened again." OPEC+ ministers will hold meetings on Sunday to decide their 2027 output policy. They face the challenge of balancing output with the United Arab Emirates no longer in the group, and ‌with Iraq and Kazakhstan pressing OPEC+ to raise its estimate ​of their oil production capacity. Two people with knowledge of the matter said OPEC+ ​may roll over its current oil output targets ​at the meeting for at least the first quarter of 2027. US crude stocks rose by ‌1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in ​the week ended November 20, ​the Energy Information Administration said. That supported prices because analysts had expected a rise of 1.5 million barrels. [EIA/S] In Asia, Thailand's Bangchak Corp said it had shut all production units at its Phra Khanong oil refinery in ​Bangkok after a fire. A drone attack ‌at the Slavyansk ECO oil refinery in Russia's southern Krasnodar region also led to a fire, ​inflicting serious damage. (Reporting by Amanda Stephenson in Calgary, Seher Dareen in London and Sudarshan Varadhan in ​Singapore; Editing by Bill Berkrot, Rod Nickel and Chris Reese)

body: There are plenty of theories about why the stock market is crashing. Some blame overvalued AI stocks or the ongoing Iran war. Others point to the controversy surrounding Nvidia's Jensen Huang or the Democratic sweep of Congress and its potential impact on data center expansion. But Brookings Institution senior fellow Robin Brooks blames the Federal Reserve. In a recent Substack post, Brooks argued that the Fed is worsening the market sell-off by signaling further rate hikes even as inflation expectations decline. Fed Governor Chris Waller, for example, said a 50-basis-point rate hike may be warranted in December to bring inflation back toward the Fed's 2% target. Meanwhile, data from Haver Analytics show that Brent crude prices and two-year inflation expectations have fallen, yet markets continue to expect higher interest rates. The result is a rise in real interest rates (nominal interest rates minus expected inflation). In effect, borrowing has become more expensive in inflation-adjusted terms, even without another Fed rate hike. "There's no doubt in my mind that the Fed is causing this meltdown," Brooks wrote. Even Wall Street's interest rate forecasts suggest the Fed may have to reverse course within a year. For example, Citigroup argues that financial markets are already signaling that interest rates are "unusually high" and will eventually need to come down. Citi expects just one more quarter-point rate hike in December, followed by a pause in early 2027 and cuts beginning in the second half of the year. It's an unusual forecast for a central bank that's supposedly still fighting inflation. The last time the Fed fought rising prices, it raised interest rates 11 times between March 2022 and July 2023, for a total increase of 5.25 percentage points. 📌 Bottom line: If Brooks is right, the Fed is making monetary policy more restrictive even before its next rate hike. And if Citi's forecast holds, investors may have to wait until the second half of 2027 for rate cuts.

The reason for the delays has not been established yet, but the cargoes were supposed to be loaded this month; now, only some of them will be loaded, and only during the first ten days of December, the report said. As a result, buyers are looking for alternatives, and Middle Eastern prices have climbed higher. One obvious possibility is that shipping oil out of the Persian Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz, which is Iraq’s only maritime route from the Gulf to the open ocean, has become a lot riskier. This possibility, while not verified by any official source, has been supported by the recent slew of reports about tankers hitting mines in Hormuz because they failed to stick to the corridor approved by Iran. Another hypothetical possibility would be a sudden drop in buyer appetite, but that possibility is not supported by the information related in the Bloomberg report, which said buyers were actually looking for prompt delivery alternatives to the Iraqi crude from the Middle East, rather than other parts of the world. Iraq has been especially hard hit by the effects of the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran. Because of its geographical position, it exports almost all of its oil via the Strait of Hormuz, and when Iran shut traffic down, Iraq had to start cutting oil production quite soon for lack of abundant storage capacity. Since then, however, production has rebounded and so have exports, on rumored deals with Iran and ship-to-ship transfers outside the Strait, in the Gulf of Oman. The latest figures show a daily average production rate of 4.6 million barrels for October, which is Iraq’s highest since 2019, and an increase of 540,000 barrels daily from September. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) stood at $84.92 the same day. Brent later spiked into the $96 range before a modest pullback, while WTI fluctuated around $85. The trigger for the rebound was the simultaneous shaking of the two pillars of Saudi crude exports. The Saudi-led coalition said on the 25th that it intercepted four drones over Ras Tanura in the Eastern Province. Damage to the refinery was not officially confirmed, but NASA satellite imagery reviewed by Reuters showed black smoke spreading across roughly 600 square kilometers around the facility. Ras Tanura is home to Saudi Arabia's largest refinery, with a capacity of 550,000 barrels a day, and an adjacent large crude export terminal. CNN, citing shipping sources, reported that loadings at the terminal were halted immediately after the attack. The following day, the 26th, Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said the Jazan refinery (400,000 barrels a day) on the Red Sea coast was hit by a projectile, killing one worker and temporarily halting part of its operations. The Houthis had earlier claimed attacks on Jeddah and Jazan ports on the Red Sea coast as well. Saudi Arabia's route for exporting crude bypassing the Strait of Hormuz runs through the Red Sea. Crude from eastern oil fields travels roughly 1,200 kilometers through the East-West Pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea coast. According to Reuters, about 4 million barrels a day flow through this pipeline, equivalent to 4% of global supply. The pipeline itself has also been targeted. Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said on the 9th that a pipeline in the Medina area was attacked, causing a limited fire but no disruption to operations. The Houthis claimed attacks on a pipeline pumping station and oil facilities in Yanbu on the 12th and on two pumping stations on the 17th, but Saudi Arabia did not confirm these. NVIDIA sets the price, supply, and timing of AI compute, which determines how fast hyperscalers, neoclouds, and frontier research labs can build. Management’s own words on the November 17 [ 1 ] earnings call support the comparison. Interim CEO Colette Kress said “demand continuing to outpace supply” [ 1 ] means NVIDIA decides allocation, and that “all are getting the same pricing.” NVIDIA also acts as a lender of sorts. It reported guarantee exposure of up to $118B [ 2 ] , including $105B tied to SB Energy’s Ohio campus hosting NVIDIA infrastructure for OpenAI, plus $390B in supply commitments. title: Inflation has shoppers hunting for value. That bodes well for Black Friday
summary: Even as consumers face macroeconomic headwinds, retailers are expecting robust holiday spending through Black Friday and beyond.
body: Economic headwinds have made consumers more cautious — but new data and reports from retailers are painting a picture of robust holiday spending through Black Friday and beyond. The macroeconomic environment has squeezed wallets. High inflation, fluctuating gas prices and labor uncertainty have dampened consumer sentiment and contributed to a pullback in spending. October's consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4%, coming in higher than expected, while the personal consumption expenditures price index accelerated to a seasonally adjusted 3.8% in October compared with last year. Meanwhile, October retail sales grew at their slowest pace in nearly a year, according to the CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor. The Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index slid to its lowest since 2014 in September, with respondents citing concerns about inflation and the job market. It's translated into caution from some retailers like Walmart and Lowe's , which have reported slower sales, smaller baskets and drops in big-ticket and discretionary purchases. Despite that pullback, recent earnings reports and end-of-year forecasts suggest consumers are still willing to shell out for the holidays. Planned spending on gifts and nongifts is estimated to be $1,049 on average this year, up 5.9% from $990 last year, according to The Conference Board. Adjusting for inflation, that figure is still up 3.2% year over year. Holiday sales are expected to top $1 trillion this year, but that growth is boosted by inflation. Though consumers have said they're willing to spend, experts have noted that shoppers are still emphasizing value and looking for deals where they can. Adobe data found that in the first 22 days of November — what it considers the beginning of the holiday season — consumers spent $82.5 billion online, marking a 9.1% year-over-year increase. That's translating to the Black Friday and Cyber Monday week, too, as consumers take advantage of deals that started days before the traditional Friday blitz. Salesforce is predicting a record-breaking holiday week between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30, as it expects online sales to reach $357 billion globally and $84 billion in the U.S., both marking 6% year-over-year increases. The report also found that retailers are offering bigger markdowns than last year, with discount rates up 8% in the U.S. in November. And according to Deloitte's Black Friday survey, participation in the shopping holiday this year is expected to be the highest seen since 2016, with 87% of shoppers reporting they plan to buy during Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales. That number is up from 82% in 2025. Consumers are expecting to spend an average of $624 this holiday, similar to last year's numbers, and Generation Z is going all in on those deals, according to Deloitte, which surveyed 1,200 consumers in mid-October. That echoes similar behavior from the cohort last year. "It's sort of the mix of feeling the squeeze on prices, people thinking about their economic condition and their financial position, but still wanting to protect the holidays," Brian McCarthy, retail strategy lead at Deloitte, told CNBC in an interview. He added that even as shoppers pulled back on spending over the past few months and delayed big purchases, that spend is now being more heavily concentrated into promotional windows like the holiday season. If households become more worried about job security, they're more likely to hold back on spending. That will then give businesses even less incentive to expand and hire. In turn, it also makes life more complicated for the ECB, which is still having to contend with elevated inflation despite pockets of economic weakness across the region. Looking to next year, I'd keep a close eye on whether the weakness in hiring starts to translate into more widespread job cuts. A more sluggish labour market is one thing but a more pronounced deterioration in employment could make Germany's economic recovery considerably harder to sustain. Probate Judge Carrie B. Markham ordered the election Monday. Organizers turned in 14,820 signatures , and the county's director of elections verified 11,065 of them, clearing the bar by 94. Atlas Development, the Buford-based company that filed the rezoning, objected to the petition on Oct. 23. Markham threw the objection out in a separate order the same day she called the election, finding that under Georgia Supreme Court precedent no party has legal standing to object to a petition filed under the Home Rule provision, and that Atlas's objection wasn't verified in any case. body: Indonesia, the largest economy in Southeast Asia, has discussed hiking the price of subsidized fuel for the first time since 2022, as the weakening local currency and persistently high oil prices weigh on government outlays for funding the subsidies. Indonesia, the world’s fourth-most populous country, hasn’t removed or reduced subsidies for gasoline and fuel amid the Strait of Hormuz crisis. The country, a net oil importer despite having domestic oil production, has subsidized fuel in one form or another since it gained independence in the 1940s. This year, the spike in oil prices has significantly raised the government’s spending on subsidizing fuels and keeping them well below market rates. Currently, gasoline and diesel are being sold in Indonesia at about half and less than a third, respectively, of their fair-value price. As a result, Indonesia’s budget has been strained, its currency, the Indonesian rupiah, has crashed to an all-time low against the U.S. dollar, and the stock market tumbled amid loss of investor confidence. Indonesia is now reportedly considering hiking the price of subsidized fuel in early 2027, in what would be the first such move since 2022, state officials and industry sources told Reuters on Friday. Indonesia last week held a meeting to discuss a potential price hike for subsidized fuels. The meeting included representatives of the economy ministry, state energy giant Pertamina, and Bank of Indonesia, the central bank, according to Reuters’ sources. However, no decision on whether to hike fuel prices has been reached at the meeting. The size of a potential increase hasn’t been discussed, either, the sources told the publication. Due to the spike in international crude oil prices, Indonesia’s government will have to spend as much as $27.2 billion (500 trillion Indonesian rupiah) on fuel subsidies this year alone. The sum would be 30% higher than the original estimate for subsidies before the Iran war hit oil supplies and hiked international oil and fuel prices. The U.S. equity markets rallied in the past days, and so did tech stocks, as risk appetite returned. This, in turn, pushed copper prices higher at the end of this week. “Recent shifts in market expectations for AI-related copper demand have been one of the important drivers of recent copper price volatility,” analysts at Mysteel said in their daily analysis today. Copper extended its recovery on Friday, ING’s commodities strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson wrote in a note early today. LME prices rebounded to above $12,600 per ton after falling below $11,500 a ton earlier in the week. The upcoming licensing round is part of South Sudan’s push to commercialize the country’s 14 available greenfield blocks and increase crude oil production from just under 170,000 barrels per day (bpd) at present to 200,000 bpd within the next two to three years, the official said at the South Sudan Oil & Power 2026 event. “We are planning to have the first licensing round and, after two to three years, have another with five additional blocks and the last with more blocks,” Minister Chuang was quoted as saying. South Sudan, a landlocked country in East Africa, broke from Sudan in 2011 and took with it around 350,000 bpd in oil production capacity at the time. Currently, South Sudan produces around 170,000 bpd of crude oil. However, the only export oil pipeline out of South Sudan passes through its neighbor to the north, Sudan. To access Port Sudan on the Red Sea, South Sudan is paying transit fees to Sudan for shipping its crude oil via the pipeline. Security issues and warring factions in Sudan and South Sudan have been major hurdles to attracting foreign investment in South Sudan’s oil industry. South Sudan aims to begin attracting investment with the licensing rounds, which will incentivize exploration. The country will also look to optimize producing fields and brownfield assets to improve recovery rates, the minister said. Technology will play a key role in South Sudan’s long-term ambition to raise its oil production to at 400,000 bpd, more than double compared to current levels. “Moving to 400,000 bpd is an ambition but it is doable. We need to challenge ourselves to use the right technologies to enhance the recovery of oil,” Chuang said. China will lead the global stockpiling in the coming months, as it typically does when oil prices fall. Beijing is also expanding its storage capacity, which could accelerate buying for storage, assuming that no escalation hikes oil prices again, according to the analyst. “Inventory refilling is a multiyear story, with 2028 being the bigger one than 2027 especially as the conflict continues for the first half at least,” Energy Aspect’s Sen told Bloomberg. “From a geopolitical point of view, we think this current status quo is the new reality,” Sen told Bloomberg. Oil prices have been below $100 per barrel over the past three weeks, but traders may have become “very complacent”, seeking to short oil. In reality, risks to supply have not eased much, according to Sen. The world is nearly out of buffers to cushion the supply shock of the Iran war, which raises the floor under oil prices each time re-escalation threatens oil supply from the Middle East. Despite numerous estimates that the Middle East’s crude oil supply is back to – and even exceeding – pre-war levels, the fundamentals show increasingly tighter markets because shipping, trade routes, and tanker costs are anything but normal. Crude oil is flowing in greater amounts, but fuel exports from the region remain severely constrained. The world entered this crisis with nearly 10 billion barrels of global oil stocks, Saudi Aramco’s CEO Amin Nasser said last month. Since then, nearly 3 billion barrels of gross oil supply were lost, or roughly half the crude and products that would normally have moved through Hormuz over the same period. “So the system is already straining. And, with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin,” Nasser warned. title: Copper price jumps most since January as short sellers retreat
summary: Traders who had bet on further declines were forced to buy back copper as the rebound in US shares lifted sentiment.
body: Traders who had bet on further declines were forced to buy back copper as the rebound in US shares lifted sentiment. London Metal Exchange. (Image by HM Treasury, Flickr , licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 2.0 .) Copper posted its biggest one-day gain in London since January on Friday, as traders who had bet on further declines scrambled to buy back positions and investors returned to riskier assets after the selloff in artificial intelligence stocks. Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange rose as much as 6.5% to above $12,600 a tonne, and is on track for its first weekly gain since early October, Bloomberg reported. In New York, Comex copper for March delivery, now the most-active contract, surged 6.3% in sympathy to touch $5.76, before giving up a good portion of the gains to trade at $5.603 a pound ($12,352 a tonne) around midday. The bounce leaves copper about 20% below its September 9 record, still technically a bear market and roughly flat for the year. The rally was probably “concentrated short-covering triggered by the rebound in US equities,” Harry Jiang, a trader at China-Base Ningbo Group, told Bloomberg. “With Chinese inventories still tight, a bounce like this makes perfect sense.” ING strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson noted that the physical market in China remains relatively firm. “Focus will remain on Chinese demand and inventories, as well as the potential movement of US-held copper,” they wrote. “Recent shifts in market expectations for AI-related copper demand have been one of the important drivers of recent copper price volatility,” analysts at Mysteel said. Data showing China’s industrial profits grew also helped. The bounce comes despite signs that metal outside China is becoming more plentiful. LME copper stocks rose to 337,925 tonnes on Thursday, up about 3% from a week earlier, and cash copper is trading close to the three-month price, with no sign of a squeeze in London. China is a different story. The Yangshan premium for imports into China hit a record $500 a tonne last week and has since eased to about $320, still well above historical levels. Copper stocks rose with the metal. Freeport-McMoRan gained 3.8% and Southern Copper 3.6% in New York, where markets close early on the day after Thanksgiving. In London, Antofagasta closed up 4.4%, Glencore 4.3%, Anglo American 3.8% and Rio Tinto 3%. Ivanhoe Mines rose 3.7% in Toronto, First Quantum Minerals 2.7% and Teck Resources 2.6%. The gains barely dent the losses since copper peaked on September 9. Ivanhoe is still down 51% since then, First Quantum 42% and Freeport 34%, while BHP has held up best among the big names, down 15%. Congo is closing the gap on Chile as the world’s biggest copper supplier. Congolese copper exports rose 8% year on year to 2.7 million tonnes in the first nine months of 2026, and quarterly shipments topped 1 million tonnes for the first time in the July-September period, government data show. Chile exported 1.28 million tonnes in the third quarter. Chile’s output is expected to fall below 5 million tonnes this year, its lowest since 2003, though that would still be about 40% higher than Congo’s 2025 production. Two CMOC mines accounted for almost 550,000 tonnes of Congo’s exports through September, while Kamoa-Kakula, owned by Ivanhoe and Zijin Mining, shipped 187,000 tonnes. Kinshasa is now pitching $15 billion of rail and other infrastructure projects to investors. A new deep-water Atlantic port opens next year, and construction is starting on the rail link from the copperbelt to Angola’s port of Lobito, Transport Minister Jean-Pierre Bemba said on Wednesday.

title: Ero Copper halts Brazil mine after water overflows
summary: Operations will resume after the local environmental agency reviews and approves a final cleanup plan developed by Ero.
body: Operations will resume after the local environmental agency reviews and approves a final cleanup plan developed by Ero. Ero Copper (TSX, NYSE: ERO) halted mining and processing at its Tucumã operation in Brazil after heavy rains overwhelmed a water collection system and state regulators found abnormal pH readings nearby. The stock dropped. Environmental authorities in Pará state initially ordered Ero to halt mining while allowing the mill to keep running, according to a company statement issued late Thursday. Processing has since stopped. Operations will resume after SEMAS, the state’s environmental agency, reviews and approves a final cleanup plan that Ero expects to file shortly. Ero gave no firm restart date or revised production forecast. “Visibility on the duration of the suspension remains limited,” Jefferies mining analyst Fahad Tariq said Friday in a note. Since Ero will probably move quickly to submit the remediation plan, “it’s possible SEMAS allows operations to restart within two weeks,” he added. Ero shares fell 6.7% to $29.97 Friday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about $3.1 billion (US$2.2 billion). The stock has traded between C$29.28 and C$56.62 in the past year. Tucumã, an open-pit mine in the Carajás mineral province that started commercial production in July 2025, was expected to produce 32,500 to 37,500 tonnes this year, or 48% of Ero’s 2026 target at the midpoint. It produced copper at a lower third-quarter cash cost than Ero’s other copper operation, Caraíba in Bahia state, at US$2.12 per lb. versus US$2.89 per pound. Assuming no production through year-end, “Tucumã would be at [the] low end of its 2026 guidance range,” Tariq said. “While a one-week interruption would have a relatively modest impact, we believe the more important consideration is the potential for prolonged downtime,” TD Securities mining analyst Craig Hutchison wrote Friday. A week offline would cost about 700 tonnes of copper output and trim TD’s forecast for Ero’s fourth-quarter earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) by about 3%, he added. Two bursts of heavy rain associated with El Niño overwhelmed pumps at a collection basin, Ero said. About 275 mm fell in the first 20 days of November, 170% more than the normal total for the full month. The company said it increased pumping and storage capacity and moved a stockpile to reduce the amount of contact water in the affected area. Pará’s environmental agency said Tuesday that inspectors found acidic industrial wastewater had reached a tributary of the Jatobá River. The agency said it increased the penalty because the company failed to notify it and civil defence authorities within the required 48 hours. Ero said it notified the agency of the overflows and put the related fines at about $2.9 million. The municipality of São Félix do Xingu separately fined Ero about $1.9 million over two reports of fish deaths. Ero said those reports predated the overflows, that it had yet to receive documentation supporting the municipal fine and that it had found no link between the deaths and Tucumã. São Félix do Xingu is located about 50 km from the mine. Tucumã accounts for 21% of Ero’s base-case net asset value , according to National Bank Financial analyst Shane Nagle. A 10-day shutdown would shave $8.4 million, or 4.3%, off his fourth-quarter EBITDA forecast, he wrote in a note. Through September, Tucumã produced 26,383 tonnes of copper in concentrate — 39% more than a year earlier. Before the shutdown, Ero expected the fourth quarter to be the mine’s strongest of the year as the mill processed more ore and recovered more of the copper in it. It had also scheduled new tailings filters for commissioning this quarter to support higher throughput in future periods.

title: Trafigura poaches Codelco commercial executive in fresh shakeup
summary: Chile’s state-owned copper giant has reshuffled its leadership as volatile metal markets and mounting operational woes bite.
body: Chile’s state-owned copper giant has reshuffled its leadership as volatile metal markets and mounting operational woes bite. Braim Chiple. ( Image courtesy of International Copper Association. ) Codelco Chief Commercial Officer Braim Chiple has resigned to join commodity trading giant Trafigura Group, the latest executive departure at the world’s largest copper producer under new CEO Jorge Gómez. Carlos Olavarría, currently Codelco’s refined copper commercial manager, will succeed Chiple on Jan. 1, the Chilean state-owned miner said Thursday. Chiple, who had led the company’s commercial operations since 2024 , will take up a role in Chile at the Singapore-based trader, three people with knowledge of the matter said. Trafigura, which recently took full control of a copper-gold project in northern Chile , declined to comment. Olavarría, who previously worked with Chiple at Anglo American, takes over at a volatile time for the global copper market. Codelco is seeking to diversify its refined copper sales after US inventories ballooned in anticipation of tariffs that have yet to materialize. Tariff uncertainty and concerns over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom have fuelled sharp swings in prices and trade flows, with metal now moving from the US towards supply-starved China . Codelco also named James Galatoire as head of projects, effective Dec. 1. Galatoire, who has led Collahuasi’s expansion project since 2024, is the latest former colleague Gómez has recruited from the mine he previously ran. Paulina Andreoli, currently risk and sustainability manager at iron ore producer Compañía Minera del Pacífico, will become general manager of Codelco’s Ventanas division on Dec. 14. Under Chairman Bernardo Fontaine, Codelco’s new leadership is prioritizing profitability and financial discipline over ambitious production growth targets as it seeks to stabilize operations, curb spending and contain debt. The miner has struggled to recover from record-low output in 2022 and 2023, with project delays, fatal accidents and declining ore grades undermining its turnaround . An internal audit also found that copper production figures had been inflated by 42,100 tonnes , potentially requiring a $140-million accounting adjustment. Codelco invested $32 billion over the past eight years even as annual copper production fell from 1.7 million tonnes to 1.2 million tonnes. Its operating costs are 78% higher than those of comparable mining operations, according to company reports. Fontaine said earlier this month that developing Codelco’s vast portfolio of untapped mining concessions through joint ventures offers the most viable route to stabilizing output. The company has already laid the groundwork for that strategy through partnerships with global miners, including Rio Tinto (ASX, LON: RIO), BHP (ASX, LON: BHP) and Anglo American (LON: AAL).

title: Gold price forecast: Fed rate hike in December may limit recovery to ₹1.30 lakh per 10 grams by 2026-end, says expert - Livemint
body: Gold prices are closely linked to US Federal Reserve interest rate decisions. The Fed's next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting is scheduled for 8-9 December 2026, with the interest rate decision expected on 9 December. The Fed last raised interest rates by 25 basis points in September, taking the federal funds target range to 3.75%–4.00%. This was its first rate hike since 2023. At its subsequent October meeting, the FOMC kept rates unchanged at 3.75%–4.00% A Fed rate hike generally puts downward pressure on gold prices. Gold is a non-interest-bearing asset and does not generate regular income, unlike bonds or bank deposits. When interest rates rise, interest-bearing investments can become more attractive to investors, reducing gold's appeal. Higher US interest rates can also strengthen the dollar and push bond yields higher, creating further pressure on gold prices. However, gold prices have recovered over the past two days, after falling to around ₹ 1.22 lakh per 10 grams from their January peak of ₹ 1.8 lakh. On 27 November, MCX December gold futures were trading at ₹ 1,25,354 per 10 grams, up 2.52%, as of 1:24 pm. With the December Fed meeting approaching, what should Indian investors expect from gold prices? And should they invest now or wait for a correction? Here's what an expert says. Gaurav Garg, Head – Research, Lemonn, a SEBI-registered online broking platform offering stocks, F&O, mutual funds and IPOs, told LiveMint that gold has recovered over the past two sessions, but the sustainability of this rebound remains uncertain. With expectations of a US Federal Reserve rate hike in December and potentially further tightening in early 2027, elevated US bond yields and a stronger dollar could continue to restrict gold’s upside, he said. He shared that higher interest rates reduced the attractiveness of non-interest-bearing assets such as gold. However, he said that continued central bank purchases, geopolitical uncertainty, and safe-haven demand should provide downside support. For Indian prices, he said that rupee depreciation against the dollar could cushion any fall in international gold prices, while rupee appreciation could add pressure. Garg said investors should avoid making lump-sum investments at a time when gold prices remain highly sensitive to interest-rate expectations. If prices rise further, existing investors can maintain their core allocation rather than chase the rally. If gold remains range-bound, systematic and staggered purchases through Gold ETFs or gold funds can help average the acquisition cost, he suggested. If prices decline further due to a stronger dollar or rising bond yields, long-term investors can gradually accumulate in phases rather than attempt to identify the exact bottom. “Central-bank demand and geopolitical uncertainty continue to support gold's long-term diversification role. title: Micron stock rebounds 6.5% as analysts forecast 45% profit growth - Crypto Briefing
body: The memory chipmaker bounced back after an oversupply scare, with analysts projecting years of rapid earnings growth tied to AI demand Micron Technology shares climbed approximately 6.5% on November 27, 2026, bringing the stock to roughly $640 after it had closed near $601 the session before. The rebound came as analysts project Micron’s profits to grow 45% per year for five consecutive years. Coverage of the move on The Motley Fool described it as an “oversold bounce” in memory chip stocks. The recovery followed a selloff driven by worries about possible oversupply in memory chips and about export restrictions. Nvidia ’s influence on the market was a key part of that concern. The numbers are large. In its fiscal fourth quarter of 2026, Micron reported record revenue of $54.2 billion, up 379% from the same quarter a year earlier. For the full 2026 fiscal year, revenue reached $133.2 billion. Gross margins hit 87%. Management’s outlook for the first quarter of fiscal 2027 calls for revenue between $60 billion and $63 billion, a midpoint of $61.5 billion. Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy. Non-GAAP EPS guidance for the quarter is $37.15 to $39.15. Even the low end is above the $33.42 Micron just posted. The driver is artificial intelligence. Demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), DRAM and NAND products is rising as companies keep building AI infrastructure. Micron has also signed multi-year customer commitments. Those agreements extend its demand visibility into the 2028 to 2030 window, and supply remains tight. Analysts have a Strong Buy consensus on Micron. Average price targets range from $1,500 to $1,625. With the stock near $640 after the bounce, even the bottom of that range is more than double the current price. Memory chips have long been among the most cyclical parts of the semiconductor industry. Producers rush to add capacity when prices rise, and that new capacity often comes online just as demand cools. What’s different this time is the kind of demand. AI infrastructure buildouts need large amounts of advanced memory, and the multi-year agreements Micron describes suggest customers want to lock in supply rather than buy on the spot market. The 379% year-over-year revenue jump in the fourth quarter shows how fast conditions changed. In the near term, the clearest checkpoint is the first quarter of fiscal 2027. Revenue inside the $60 billion to $63 billion range, with EPS in the guided band, would support the bullish case. A 6.5% one-day move for a company this large shows how quickly sentiment can swing when a stock trades on long-range forecasts as much as on current results. body: What a week. Gold briefly touched a 15-month low on Wednesday before rallying nearly 3% on Friday. Silver is up around 7% over the week, having plunged well below $40 on Wednesday. What drove these sharp price swings, and what do they tell us about the outlook for the months ahead? Anyone following the gold price this week will have witnessed some dramatic swings. On Monday, Nvidia brought back its chief executive, Jensen Huang, prompting a rally in equity markets. Gold rose by 2.7% and silver by 4.7%. The rally was short-lived, however, as renewed doubts over the AI boom and reports of new US import tariffs pushed gold down 2.2% and silver down 5.2% on Tuesday. We covered the events of those first few days in our in-depth market update on Wednesday. Wednesday marked the low point. Following strong US economic growth and inflation figures, gold fell to an intraday low of $3,426 per troy ounce, its lowest level since August 2025. Silver plunged to $38.09. Yet both metals managed to close higher that day as Wall Street recovered. US stock markets were closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday, making for a quiet trading session. Daily price movements in gold and silver in November (source: Kitco) Friday finally brought some relief. Technology stocks continued their recovery, while Chinese equities surged following a rare pledge of government support . Beijing reassured investors by promising to actively support the stock market, including through share purchases by state-backed funds. This gave gold and silver an additional boost. Chinese investors hold relatively large amounts of gold and silver , and when equity markets fall, they often draw on these reserves, creating selling pressure. As trading in China gets under way in the middle of the night in the Netherlands, any easing of that pressure is often reflected in the gold price early in the European morning. Gold rose nearly 3% on Friday morning to around $3,668 (just over €107,700 per kilogram), while silver climbed more than 6% to $44. Over the week as a whole, gold is up nearly 4% and silver around 7%. Gold is often used as an “ATM”, or cash machine, during periods of market stress, according to Ole Hansen (source: Ole Hansen on X ) . What explains such dramatic swings? The answer lies less in gold itself than in the wider financial markets. As Koen Lauwers explained in Thursday’s market update , there was a widespread scramble for liquidity. Investors who have borrowed money to invest and are nursing losses on equities need to raise cash quickly. They therefore sell whatever is easiest to liquidate, and that is often gold. When equity markets recover, that selling pressure subsides and gold rebounds just as sharply. The recovery “highlights the role of precious metals as an ATM in times of market stress”, wrote Ole Sloth Hansen, Head of Commodity Strategy at Saxo Bank, in a post on X . With AI-related stocks recovering and risk appetite returning, “the queue at the cash machine appears to be thinning”, easing selling pressure on both metals. Beneath all this volatility lies an interest rate outlook that has become more hawkish rather than less so this week. PCE inflation, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, stood at 3.8% in October. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, rose to 3.3%. title: Kazakhstan’s 2027 Outlook Improves as Inflation Forecast Falls, Tenge Strengthens - The Astana Times
body: By Dana Omirgazy in Business , Editor’s Picks on 27 November 2026 ASTANA – Analysts have revised their forecasts for Kazakhstan’s inflation, exchange rate and export revenues upward, while slightly lowering expectations for economic growth this year, according to the National Bank of Kazakhstan’s November macroeconomic survey released on Nov. 26. The survey, conducted on Nov. 12-18 among 15 financial, rating and research organizations, suggests a more favorable near-term economic outlook, although longer-term risks remain. Analysts raised their 2026 average Brent crude oil price forecast from $88.4 to $93.3 per barrel, while maintaining projections of $80 in 2027 and $75 in 2028. Despite higher oil price expectations, Kazakhstan’s 2026 economic growth forecast was lowered from 4.8% to 4.6%. The 2027 projection remained unchanged at 4.7%, while the 2028 estimate edged up from 4.4% to 4.5%. The figures suggest that favorable oil prices may support export revenues without necessarily translating into faster economic growth. The inflation forecast for 2026 was revised downward from 9.5% to 9.1%, while the 2027 projection declined from 8.3% to 8%. Inflation is expected to reach 7% in 2028, slightly above the previous estimate of 6.9%. Analysts also anticipate a gradual reduction in the National Bank’s base rate, from an expected 15.8% at the end of 2026 to 13.4% in 2027 and 10.8% in 2028. Meanwhile, exchange rate expectations improved across the entire forecast period. The average exchange rate is projected at 472 tenge per U.S. dollar in 2026, compared with the previous forecast of 479 tenge. The estimates for 2027 and 2028 were revised to 489.8 and 510.4 tenge per dollar, respectively, from 499.6 and 527.1. Despite these upward revisions, analysts still expect the national currency to weaken gradually in nominal terms over the coming years. The forecast for Kazakhstan’s exports of goods and services in 2026 increased from $96 billion to $101 billion, while the 2027 estimate rose from $93.9 billion to $100 billion. However, the projected positive gap between exports and imports is expected to narrow significantly, from $17.2 billion in 2026 to $11.8 billion in 2027 and $5.6 billion in 2028. This trend suggests that declining oil prices and rising imports could gradually reduce the support that foreign trade provides to the tenge. Commenting on the survey on his Tengenomika Telegram channel, economic analyst Ruslan Sultanov described the November results as presenting a relatively favorable near-term outlook. However, he cautioned that declining oil prices, rising imports and gradually easing monetary conditions increase the importance of productivity, export diversification and domestic sources of economic growth. Long-term expectations remain broadly stable, with potential economic growth projected at 4.5% and inflation at 5.1% over a five-year horizon. Nevertheless, wide ranges in medium-term forecasts indicate persistent economic uncertainty.

However, gold has since late November experienced a significant correction. International prices briefly fell below $3,500 on November 25, reaching a 15-month low, before recovering to $3,591.37 per ounce on November 26. Fine gold traded at NRs 242,800 per tola on the same day, down by NRs 96,500 from its January peak. The decline has raised questions about gold’s traditional role as a safe-haven asset. Although concerns over government debt, currency depreciation and geopolitical tensions continue to support gold’s long-term appeal, changing monetary conditions and investor behaviour have put significant pressure on prices. During the COVID-19 pandemic, low interest rates and heightened economic uncertainty drove gold prices above $2,000 per ounce. In the post-pandemic period, persistent inflation, geopolitical tensions, rising government debt concerns, and central banks’ efforts to diversify their reserves have further fueled the recent surge in gold prices. In 2025, global gold demand reached a record 5,002 tonnes, says the World Gold Council , supported by central bank purchases of 863 tonnes and gold ETF inflows of 801 tonnes. body: Singapore is reportedly in talks with the United States to maintain access to advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips after Washington tightened export restrictions, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said Friday. Speaking at the Asia Future Summit, Gan said Singapore was reviewing its procedures to prevent illicit semiconductor trading and would continue working with US authorities to address their concerns, Bloomberg reported on Friday. “We have not confirmed it,” Gan said when asked about reports that Nvidia ( NVDA ) had stopped shipments to Southeast Asia. He added that the government was engaging businesses to assess the impact of the restrictions and would continue working with Washington to help Singaporean companies maintain access to high-end chips. The US Commerce Department introduced new export controls effective November 19, requiring licenses for shipments of covered advanced semiconductors to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. Washington identified these countries as posing a higher-than-normal risk of chip diversion. The rules also restrict shipments of advanced chips to overseas data centers that provide significant computing power remotely to companies headquartered in China and certain other restricted destinations. The measures include an exemption from the five-country licensing requirement for chips destined for US-headquartered companies, subject to reporting conditions. Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said last week that he expected the restrictions to affect some of the high-end chip shipments passing through the city-state, Bloomberg reported. The Financial Times reported Thursday that Nvidia manufacturing partners, including Super Micro Computer ( SMCI ) and Dell Technologies ( DELL ), had informed buyers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia that their orders could not be shipped. Singapore's government has not independently confirmed the reported suspension, the report said, citing three people familiar with the matter. The developments come amid investigations involving Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed International and its former executive Alice Huang. Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said on November 12 that police had investigated Huang over suspected false declarations involving server purchases but found insufficient evidence to establish that she had committed those offenses. Authorities issued her a stern warning for knowingly providing inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed and barred her from re-entering Singapore. The ministry said the investigation into Megaspeed remained ongoing and that Huang had not been investigated for espionage. Singapore has maintained that it does not enforce other countries' unilateral export controls but will take action against companies that breach its own laws through fraud or dishonest practices. Gan said the government would continue discussions with the U.S. while working with businesses to determine how the latest restrictions affect their operations. However, he does not expect the hearings themselves to have a significant impact on the company’s stock price in the short term. “This is just the first salvo in a series of events that will continue for at least a year, and the market is already pricing in a host of potential surprises,” Blank said in a comment to MarketWatch. In his view, Huang’s testimony could have implications for the entire semiconductor industry if he reveals additional details about shipments of advanced chips to China . At the same time, Huang understands the seriousness of his situation and will try to remain reserved during his testimony before lawmakers, Blank believes. “To some extent, the events of the past two weeks have made him more humble, and I expect him to take what’s happening seriously and speak quite frankly. title: Jensen Huang's Comeback Rally Fizzles as S&P Places Nvidia on Negative Watch, Though Analysts Still See a Buying Opportunity - BigGo Finance
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's return lasted barely a day before market enthusiasm quickly faded. After Nvidia shares surged 31.48% on the 23rd on news of Huang's reinstatement, adding roughly $1 trillion in market value in a single session, the stock weakened over the next two trading days. On the 25th, it plunged more than 8% intraday to a low of $141.17 before closing down 3.91% at $149.30. Over the two sessions, the stock gave back a combined $15.75, about 40% of the 23rd's single-day gain of $39.52, but still above the $125.53 closing price on November 20, before Huang's reinstatement. Meanwhile, S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia's AA credit rating on negative credit watch, with a possible one-notch downgrade within 90 days, adding uncertainty to the AI chip leader's outlook. The same roller-coaster played out in Taiwanese stocks. After news of Huang's reinstatement emerged, Taiwan's weighted index surged 3,310.46 points, or 8.99%, to close at 40,122.35 on the 24th, marking the largest single-day point gain in history, with TSMC (2330) opening limit-up at NT$2,230. But as Nvidia weakened for two straight days in U.S. markets and U.S. tariff concerns resurfaced, Taiwan's index plunged as much as 3,440.45 points intraday on the 25th before closing down 1,926.92 points, or 4.80%, at 38,195.43 — the sixth-largest closing point drop in history — and fell below its annual line of about 39,551. TSMC closed down NT$80. In total, Taiwanese stocks gave back nearly 60% of the 24th's gains over two trading days. The root of the turmoil is Huang's extramarital affair scandal. The affair reportedly involved at least one subordinate and a woman who had previously been investigated by the U.S. government on suspicion of espionage activities on behalf of China; Nvidia's dealings with China and whether it complied with chip export controls are also under continued scrutiny. Huang resigned and returned within just 11 days. The board had publicly stated in mid-November that it had no intention of reinstating him as CEO, but after Donald Trump publicly said he personally intervened and lobbied the board, the board reversed course, voting unanimously on the 22nd to bring him back and announcing the decision on the 23rd. However, Huang's return did not eliminate credit rating agencies' concerns about corporate governance. S&P noted that information related to the CEO and concerns about possible export control violations exposed weaknesses in Nvidia's management and governance structure, particularly the board's structure, composition and oversight effectiveness. S&P also downgraded Nvidia's management and governance assessment from "positive" to "neutral" and said it would meet with the board and management to discuss board independence, effective oversight of the CEO and a credible succession plan. S&P said it expects any downgrade to be limited to one notch unless Nvidia's operating outlook deteriorates; however, if investigations or disclosures show that Nvidia circumvented export controls, or that its disclosures of exposure to China and neighboring regions were misleading or understated, its credit quality would be further affected. Moody's, after Huang's departure, had already revised Nvidia's rating outlook from "positive" to "stable" on November 18, keeping its Aa1 rating unchanged, and did not adjust again on the 25th when S&P acted — meaning the two agencies gave different readings on Nvidia. Moody's also warned that governance and regulatory uncertainty remained unresolved after Huang's return, and that regulators and the government remain highly focused on Nvidia, which could distract management. Downgrade concerns were directly reflected in the bond market. About $32.5 billion of Nvidia bonds are included in the U.S. investment-grade corporate bond index.
